title: Communication SaaS - 0 to 1 B2B SaaS product design
meta_description: A product design case study: 0 to 1 product design for a US-based B2B SaaS platform that lets organizations build and schedule voice-message episodes for their subscribers.

blocks.title: Designing **Communication SaaS**, a 0 to 1 B2B messaging platform.
blocks.subtitle: End-to-end product design for a US-based B2B SaaS platform that lets organizations build voice-message episodes and schedule them out to their subscribers.

blocks.title: Two very different audiences, one product.
body: Communication SaaS is a B2B platform built around a simple idea: an organization records short voice messages for the people it serves, and those people receive them as an easy, familiar listening experience, no app-hunting, no logging into a portal to read a wall of text.

That simple idea splits the product in two. On one side, an admin working on behalf of an organization needs to assemble, review, and schedule a sequence of voice messages before anything goes out. On the other, a subscriber just wants to press play. Designing for both sides inside a single system, without either one feeling like an afterthought, was the core of this engagement.

blocks.title: Turning a sequence of voice clips into a timeline you can actually edit.
body: The heart of the admin side is the Episode Builder, step two of a three-step flow (Basic Information, Episode Builder, Approval and Schedule). Rather than presenting a flat list of uploaded clips, messages are laid out on a horizontal timeline with real durations, so an admin can see exactly how a 55-minute episode is composed before it ever reaches a subscriber.

Each message is its own card on the timeline, with inline playback, so reviewing content doesn't mean leaving the builder to open a separate file. A dedicated add-slot keeps the door open for building the episode out further, and the whole timeline is zoomable, useful once an episode has more than a handful of segments.

images.alt: Episode Builder step with a horizontal message timeline
Zoomed-in view of the episode timeline with individual message cards

blocks.title: A library that scales past the first few messages.
body: Organizations don't build one episode and stop, they build a library: welcome messages, weekly updates, seasonal content, drafts waiting on approval. The Library view gives admins a searchable, filterable table across every segment they've created, with client, status (Draft, Under review, Scheduled, Published), publish date, and last-used timestamp visible at a glance, plus quick actions to preview, edit, or remove a segment without drilling into it first.

images.alt: Library table listing message segments with status and client columns

blocks.title: Borrowing a mental model people already trust.
body: For the subscriber side, the design decision was to lean into a format people already know how to use: a podcast player. Episodes show up with a title, date, standard transport controls, playback speed, and a scrubber, exactly the pattern anyone who listens to podcasts already has muscle memory for.

Underneath the player sits a full transcript, broken into labeled sections, so a subscriber who'd rather scan than listen isn't stuck. That transcript view also does double duty as an accessibility path for anyone who can't or doesn't want to listen to audio in the moment they receive it.

images.alt: Subscriber mobile podcast player with episode transcript

items.title: Two audiences means two design systems living in one product
items.body: The admin side needed density and control, timelines, tables, multi-step approval. The subscriber side needed the opposite, one obvious action and nothing else competing for attention. Both had to feel like they came from the same company.

items.title: Approval workflows are a design surface, not just a backend concern
items.body: A three-step episode flow with an explicit approval stage isn't just process, it's a trust signal for organizations sending messages to real people. Making that stage visible in the UI, not hidden in a status field, mattered.

items.title: Familiar mental models lower the cost of adoption
items.body: Building the subscriber experience around a podcast player instead of a custom messaging inbox meant almost no onboarding was needed. People already knew how to use it before they opened it for the first time.
